Cipher has years of potential growth ahead if it can convert that power into long-term AI leases, with about 4 GW of the pipeline targeted for 2028 and beyond.

text:
$CIFR already has ~700 MW contracted for AI and HPC with another ~4.4 GW in its power pipeline which is more than 6x what it has signed today.

Cipher has years of potential growth ahead if it can keep turning that power into long term AI leases with ~4 GW of its pipeline targeted for 2028 and beyond.

zh_summary: @alphatrends 表示，雖然他相信 $NKE 已經見底，但他以 35.50 美元賣出了三分之一的持倉（買入價 33 美元）。風險管理比他對底部的信念更重要。他寧願鎖定部分獲利，以免股價回落時顯得愚蠢，若回調可能在更低價位買回。被引用的貼文指出他仍持有部分長線倉位。

text:
Even though I believe $NKE has made a low, I sold 1/3 of my position (bought at $33) at $35.50. 

Risk management matters more to me than my conviction on the bottom. 

I’d rather lock in some gains and avoid feeling foolish if the stock drops back down. If it pulls back, I may look to rebuy what I sold at a lower price.

name: Tobias Carlisle
zh_summary: @Greenbackd：優質債券只能防範某一類崩盤。在最近兩個截然不同的壓力年份，各類股票均下跌，國際股票及房地產在兩次崩盤中都未能保護美國投資者。
en_summary: @Greenbackd: high quality bonds protect against one kind of crash but not another. In the two recent stress years, stocks of every kind fell, and international stocks and real estate did not protect US investors in either.
ko_summary: @Greenbackd: 우량 채권은 한 종류의 폭락만 막는다. 최근 두 번의 스트레스 해에 모든 주식이 하락했고 해외 주식과 부동산은 어느 쪽에서도 미국 투자자를 보호하지 못했다.
text:
If high-quality bonds protect against one kind of crash but not the other, what else belongs in the portfolio? Many products are sold as crash protection. The fairest test is to see what each did in the two most recent, very different stress years.

The chart repays careful reading.

* Stocks of every kind fell in both years. International stocks and real estate did not protect U.S. investors in either crash. Their case rests on long-run diversification, not crash protection. Within U.S. stocks, value shares held up far better than growth shares in 2022, but not in 2008.

* Long-term Treasuries and commodities are mirror images. Each saved the portfolio in one year and hurt it badly in the other. Holding a modest amount of both is a hedge against not knowing which engine will run.

* Gold roughly held its value in both years. It pays no income, and it can fall sharply in other periods, as it did in the early 1980s and in 2013. It is a store of value in a crisis, not a growth engine. 

*Managed futures gained in both years. These funds follow price trends across stocks, bonds, currencies, and commodities, going long or short. They tend to do well in extended declines of any kind. They can also lag for years in calm, trendless markets, and their fees are higher than index funds’.

*Treasury bills gained in both years. Its cost is low returns in good times.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said investors trade more on what they think the Fed will do than on what it should do, a view that sits uneasily with Kevin Warsh's push to say less about the outlook in pursuit of a purer market signal. 

"Having been on the market side of things for three decades, I think that what markets are looking for is they're looking for any guidance as to where the Fed is going to go. I know that bankers, investment professionals, their number one goal is to produce returns for themselves and their clients. That's their goal, that's the job. And to do that, they both want to look at what the fundamentals of the economy are doing and what they're saying, but I think they respond more based on what they think the Fed will do rather than what they think we should do. And so I think that it's important to take signal back from the markets about how the economy is progressing, but I take more signal about how the economy is progressing from the data, from the stories I hear in the district."

Unitree's CEO, who in August saw a robotics "ChatGPT moment" taking two to three years or up to a decade, now expects it within 1 or 2 years after testing GPT-6, defined as robots doing about 80% of tasks in 80% of unfamiliar environments. text:
Physical AI + Humanoids are the next progression of AI.

$NVDA CES 2025 projections and Elon's prediction on $TSLA + 1 Billion humanoids in the next decade, seems to be speeding up. 

New statement from Unitree CEO after testing GPT-6 on their humanoid program was that:

- In August, before GPT-6's release, Wang said the industry could take two to three years at its fastest pace, or as long as a decade, to reach its "ChatGPT moment"

- Now, OpenAI's GPT-6 model prompted expectations that a breakthrough could happen "within 1 or 2 years"

- He defined that moment as robots being able to complete around 80 per cent of tasks in 80 per cent of unfamiliar environments using voice or text commands.

- "It's possible that, say, a GPT-7 model released next year could directly crack the problems of embodied intelligence"

- "The whole embodied intelligence industry has been shaken up after the release of GPT-6"

Just looking at some benchmarks on robotic hand manipulation, "On the bowl task Astra placed the block in 19 of 20 trials, against Fable 5.1's 8 of 20".

But for the puzzle task "Astra completed the insertion 2 times in 20 against Fable 5.1's 2 in 20"".. so we're getting there. 

But going from 2-3 years (potentially to a decade), and compressing that down to 1 or 2 years (to achieve 80%+ of tasks in unfamiliar environemnts) is a significant change in outlook.

text:
UBS sees 2027 as the inflection year for $CBRS with revenue growing ~4x to $3.3B before reaching ~$23B by 2030 with 46% operating margins.

The interesting part is Cerebras’s on chip memory advantage becomes way more valuable as AI agents make dozens of model calls per task with CS-5 targeting 10K tokens per second per user in 2027.

And with ~$25B in contracted backlog already equivalent to nearly half of projected revenue from 2027 through 2030, shares now trade below 20x 2028 earnings.

$MU $SNDK

Are the CXMT memory optimization headlines a real threat to the memory trade or is it just another architecture that will lead to more usage of tokens which will make up for pricing power in volumes?

The memory trade, like the semis in general, has been fragile enough for these headlines to affect them almost every week.

We saw this last week with the HDD manufacturing capacity increase by Toshiba that took $STX and $WDC down 20%. 

At some point, the street either is going to believe these names are undervalued relative to their growth or they are going to give up on trying to be optimistic when a new headline around memory efficiency comes out every other week and reminds them about how traditionally cyclical the business is.

text:

And I think Bill Ackman has the better map of how this ends.

Burry's Oct 11 note is clear: he sold the common, bought junior preferred, and flagged a Treasury conversion of the senior preferred (SPS) into common — dilution of 90%+.

That risk is real on paper.
I just don't think it's the base case the Trump team is trying to deliver.

Here's why I side with Ackman:

1. The SPS has already been paid — economically.

Fannie and Freddie drew about $193B from Treasury after 2008.
They have since returned about $301B in dividends.

Ackman's point is simple: treat the senior preferred as repaid, don't invent a brand-new dilution event to wipe out private common holders.

2. Ackman's path preserves the common.

His three-step plan:
→ Treasury / FHFA amend the PSPA so the SPS is treated as satisfied
→ Treasury exercises its warrants for ~79.9% of the common
→ Relist on the NYSE while conservatorship continues

Government control stays.
Mortgage markets aren't disrupted.
Existing common isn't vaporized by a 90% conversion.

That is "walk before you run," not "convert and crush."

Burry's move makes sense if you believe Wall Street's conversion base case wins.
